title: fix(mr): warn when publishing --reviewer-state on your own merge request
description:
## Description

`glab mr note publish --reviewer-state ...` silently did nothing when the caller is the MR author: GitLab's `bulk_publish` endpoint returns 204 but discards the result of `MergeRequests::UpdateReviewerStateService`, which fails with a swallowed "Reviewer not found" because an author cannot be a reviewer of their own merge request. The drafts were published, but the review state was never set and no diagnostic was shown.

This MR detects the case client-side: when `--reviewer-state` is set, publish does a best-effort `CurrentUser` lookup and, if the user authored the MR, prints a warning to stderr:

```
! GitLab ignores --reviewer-state on your own merge request; your review state will not be set.
```

Publishing itself still succeeds, the field is still sent, and the exit code is unchanged — only the state is ignored server-side. On a `CurrentUser` lookup error the warning is skipped so the extra call can never fail the publish. The `--reviewer-state` paragraph in the command's `Long` help documents the limitation.

## Related Issues

Resolves #8564

## How has this been tested?

- Reproduced the issue end-to-end against a GDK instance (`gdk.test:3000`): publish as the MR author with `--reviewer-state reviewed` returned exit 0 with no warning, and the `/reviewers` readback stayed `[]`.
- After the fix, the same flow emits the warning on stderr while stdout/exit code are unchanged; a bare `mr note publish` produces no stderr output; publishing with `--reviewer-state` as a non-author emits no warning.
- New unit subtests in `mr_note_publish_test.go`: author warns, non-author does not; both assert `ReviewerState` is still sent. Both fail before the fix. The existing bare-publish subtest sets no `CurrentUser` expectation, proving no extra API call without the flag.
- `docs/source/mr/note/publish.md` regenerated with `make gen-docs`.

title: fix(issuable): validate output flag enums and trim changelog version tag
description:
### Problem
1. In `glab issue list` / `glab mr list` / `glab release list`, passing an invalid argument to `-O, --output` or `-F, --output-format` (e.g. `--output invalid`) passed the invalid string downstream instead of validating allowed flag choices up front.
2. In `glab changelog generate`, `git.DescribeByTags()` output contained a trailing newline, causing 422 Unprocessable Entity HTTP errors when querying GitLab release endpoints.

### Fix
1. Registered `-O, --output` and `-F, --output-format` flags with `cmdutils.NewEnumValue` across `issuable` list commands to enforce allowed flag enums (`text`, `json`) at CLI parse time.
2. Updated `git.DescribeByTags()` in `internal/git/git.go` to trim leading/trailing whitespace (`strings.TrimSpace`).

### Tests Performed
- Added `TestIssueList_InvalidOutputFlags` in `internal/commands/issuable/list/issuable_list_test.go` covering flag validation errors for invalid `--output` and `--output-format` values.
- Verified unit test suite in Docker container `golang:latest` (Go 1.27.1) — 100% PASS.

Closes #8547
Closes #8387

title: feat(theme): add per-role color overrides for accessibility
description:
## What

Adds eight `theme_color_*` config keys (and matching `GLAB_THEME_COLOR_*` env vars): `orange`, `purple`, `blue`, `green`, `red`, `warning`, `text`, `subtle` — one per role in `theme.GitLabColors`. Each takes a `#RRGGBB` hex value and overrides the built-in color for that role only; unset roles keep the built-in value.

No new command, no theme file, no registry — this is the override mechanism alone, per !3955's discussion.

**Stacked on !3955** (`fix(iostreams): make background/color detection reachable, add --color mode`) — merge that one first.

## Why: WCAG 2.2, not "similar to other tools"

A single built-in palette, however well audited for one background, cannot guarantee sufficient contrast or a usable hue for every user:

- **SC 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum, AA)** requires 4.5:1; **SC 1.4.6 (Contrast Enhanced, AAA)** requires 7:1 for users who need more than AA provides. A palette that clears AA against its assumed background can still fail a user who needs AAA-level contrast.
- SC 1.4.3's own rationale notes that hue perception varies by color vision deficiency independent of luminance contrast, and specifically calls out avoiding red-on-black for protanopia. A palette tuned for one deficiency can still be unusable for another.
- **SC 1.4.1 (Use of Color)** matters here because glab assigns color to semantic roles (success/error/warning), not decoratively. A user who can't distinguish two of those hues needs to remap the specific role, not swap the whole theme.
- `--color=16` (from !3955) doesn't cover this: it defers to the terminal's generic ANSI slots, but glab's role-to-hue mapping is its own layer on top of that, and a shared terminal theme can't disambiguate glab-specific semantic roles the way a per-role override can.

WCAG's own understanding doc for 1.4.3 explicitly encourages authors to provide a mechanism for users to adjust foreground/background colors when the built-in choice doesn't meet their needs. Eight independent, optional config keys are that mechanism: zero cost to the default experience, no code/CLI surface for anyone who doesn't need it.

**Deliberately out of scope:** validating the resulting contrast ratio against WCAG's own formula when an override is set. That's real, separate work (compute relative luminance, decide what to do when a chosen override fails AA/AAA against a detected background that itself isn't always knowable) — this MR is the override mechanism only.

## What changed

- `internal/theme/overrides.go`: `ParseColorOverride` (validates `#RRGGBB`, rejects anything else including empty/shorthand/named colors) and `ApplyOverrides` (layers a `GitLabColors` of overrides onto a base `GitLabColors`, role by role).
- `FangColorScheme` takes a `GitLabColors` overrides parameter now. Its `ErrorHeader` background was hardcoded to the light-mode red hex regardless of dark/light detection or overrides; it now reads `colors.Red` like everything else in the function, so it follows a `Red` override and also picks up the dark-mode red variant it should already have been using. Calling this out explicitly since it's an incidental default-rendering change, not just override plumbing.
- `internal/iostreams`: new `colorOverrides` field, `WithColorOverrides` option, applied in `colorPalette()` alongside the existing `ColorMode` handling from !3955.
- `cmd/glab/main.go`: `resolveColorOverrides` reads the eight config keys once, parses each (invalid/unset values silently fall back to the built-in color — matching this codebase's existing convention of not failing a command over a malformed value in a purely cosmetic setting), and the result feeds both `IOStreams` and fang's `ColorSchemeFunc`.

## Testing

New tests in `internal/theme/overrides_test.go`, `internal/iostreams/color_test.go`, `cmd/glab/main_test.go`. Full test suite passes for every affected package (`theme`, `iostreams`, `config`, `cmd/glab`, `commands`) with no regressions.

Manually verified against a built binary: `config set theme_color_red '#FF00FF'` persists and reads back; `GLAB_THEME_COLOR_GREEN` overrides the config value; an active override doesn't affect any other role or crash rendering.

`make gen-docs` run; regenerated docs add the eight new config keys and env vars.

title: fix(build): exclude posix fsx tests from windows builds
description:
## Description

This merge request fixes a build failure that prevents developers from compiling and running tests on Windows locally.

Running `go test ./...` on Windows fails with `undefined: syscall.Stat_t` and `undefined: renameio` errors in `internal/dependencyfirewall/fsx/fsx_test.go` and `internal/fsx/fsx_test.go`. These files contain tests that rely on POSIX-specific atomic replace semantics, file permissions, and `syscall.Stat_t`. Even if the tests themselves contain `if runtime.GOOS == "windows" { t.Skip() }`, the Go compiler still attempts to type-check the entire file and crashes because those structs do not exist in the Windows OS kernel.

This MR updates the build constraints in `internal/dependencyfirewall/fsx/fsx_test.go` to include `!windows` so the file is properly ignored by the Go compiler on Windows. It also extracts the purely POSIX-specific tests from `internal/fsx/fsx_test.go` into a new `write_unix_test.go` file (with a `!windows` tag), allowing the remaining OS-agnostic tests to successfully compile and run on Windows.

## Related Issues

Resolves #8551

## How has this been tested?

1. Ran `go test ./...` locally on Windows.
2. Verified that `internal/dependencyfirewall/fsx` is safely skipped (`[no test files]`).
3. Verified that `internal/fsx` passes the remaining tests in 0.208s.
4. Confirmed the build completes successfully without `syscall.Stat_t` errors.
